Biology.question: Explain briefly the reason why energy flow in an ecosystem is non-cyclic.
Biology.questionHtml: Explain briefly the reason why energy flow in an ecosystem is non-cyclic.
Biology.answerText: Energy flow in an ecosystem is non-cyclic because it follows a one-way path. It starts from the sun. Energy is transferred through different trophic levels/from one organism to another. It reduces across each trophic level. It is eventually lost as heat to the environment, without returning to any of the trophic levels.

English-Language.question: Write an article suitable for publication in your school magazine discussing three measures that students should take to protect themselves against malaria.
English-Language.questionHtml: Write an article suitable for publication in your school magazine discussing three measures that students should take to protect themselves against malaria.
English-Language.answerText: Here is a school magazine article suitable for WAEC/NECO standards: THREE MEASURES STUDENTS SHOULD TAKE TO PROTECT THEMSELVES AGAINST MALARIA Malaria remains one of the most common diseases affecting students in our country. It is caused by parasites transmitted through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Every year, thousands of students miss classes, examinations, and other important school activities because of malaria. Since prevention is better than cure, students must take deliberate steps to protect themselves against this dangerous disease. Three important measures that students should adopt are the regular use of insecticide-treated mosquito nets, maintaining a clean environment, and seeking prompt medical attention whenever symptoms appear. The first measure is the consistent use of insecticide-treated mosquito nets. Mosquitoes are most active at night, and many people become infected while sleeping. Sleeping under a treated mosquito net provides a protective barrier between the individual and mosquitoes. In addition, the insecticide on the net kills or repels mosquitoes that come into contact with it. Students should therefore ensure that they sleep under properly installed mosquito nets every night. This simple habit can greatly reduce the chances of contracting malaria. Another important measure is maintaining a clean environment. Mosquitoes breed in stagnant water found in gutters, discarded containers, puddles, and other dirty surroundings. Students should regularly clean their homes and school environments by clearing bushes, disposing of refuse properly, and ensuring that drains are free from blockage. Water storage containers should also be covered to prevent mosquitoes from laying eggs in them. By keeping the environment clean, students can significantly reduce mosquito breeding and the spread of malaria. The third measure is seeking prompt medical attention whenever symptoms of malaria occur. Common symptoms include fever, headache, body weakness, loss of appetite, and chills. Some students ignore these signs or engage in self-medication, which may worsen their condition. Instead, they should visit a qualified health centre for proper diagnosis and treatment. Early treatment not only prevents complications but also helps students recover quickly and return to their academic activities. In conclusion, malaria is a serious health challenge, but it can be prevented through conscious efforts. The regular use of insecticide-treated mosquito nets, proper environmental sanitation, and prompt medical attention are three effective measures that students should adopt. If every student follows these precautions, the incidence of malaria will reduce considerably, leading to better health and improved academic performance.

English-Language.questionHtml: You are the main speaker in a debate competition on the topic: Technical and vocational education should be mandatory in secondary schools. Write your arguments for or against the motion.
English-Language.answerText: You're right. In a debate, the speaker's name is usually introduced naturally in the opening rather than as a separate byline. TECHNICAL AND VOCATIONAL EDUCATION SHOULD BE MANDATORY IN SECONDARY SCHOOLS Mr Chairman, Panel of Judges, Accurate Timekeeper, Co-debaters, Ladies and Gentlemen. My name is Daniel Nancy, and I stand before you today to strongly support the motion which states that technical and vocational education should be mandatory in secondary schools. Technical and vocational education refers to the training that equips students with practical skills in areas such as carpentry, tailoring, electrical installation, plumbing, welding, agriculture, computer maintenance, catering, and many other occupations. Making such education compulsory in secondary schools will bring numerous benefits to students and society at large. My first argument is that technical and vocational education promotes self-reliance. One of the major challenges facing many young people today is unemployment. Every year, thousands of school leavers search endlessly for white-collar jobs that are either scarce or unavailable. If students are equipped with vocational skills while still in secondary school, they can establish their own businesses and earn a living without depending entirely on government employment. A student who learns tailoring, catering, or computer repairs can become an entrepreneur and even employ others. Secondly, technical and vocational education contributes significantly to national development. No nation can develop without skilled manpower. Countries that are technologically advanced place great emphasis on technical education because it produces craftsmen, technicians, and innovators who drive industrial growth. By making vocational education mandatory, schools will produce graduates who possess practical skills that can support manufacturing, construction, agriculture, and other productive sectors of the economy. Thirdly, vocational education helps students discover and develop their talents. Not every student is academically inclined. Some students possess exceptional practical abilities that may not be adequately reflected through conventional classroom learning. Technical education provides such students with opportunities to identify their strengths and excel in areas where they have natural abilities. This encourages confidence, creativity, and productivity. Furthermore, technical and vocational education reduces poverty and crime. Many young people become involved in criminal activities because they lack employable skills and legitimate means of earning income. When students acquire vocational competencies, they are better positioned to engage in productive ventures and contribute positively to society. Skill acquisition therefore serves as a powerful tool for economic empowerment and social stability. In addition, vocational training prepares students for the realities of modern society. The world is increasingly becoming skill-driven. Employers now seek individuals who can apply practical knowledge to solve problems. Students who receive vocational education gain hands-on experience that makes them more adaptable and competitive in the labour market. Those opposing this motion may argue that making vocational education compulsory will increase the workload of students and schools. However, the benefits far outweigh any temporary challenges. With proper planning, qualified instructors, and adequate facilities, vocational education can be successfully integrated into the secondary school curriculum without disrupting academic learning. In conclusion, technical and vocational education should be mandatory in secondary schools because it promotes self-reliance, fosters national development, helps students discover their talents, reduces unemployment and crime, and prepares young people for the demands of the modern world. I therefore urge this distinguished audience to support the motion wholeheartedly. Thank you for listening.

English-Language.answerText: STATEMENT TO THE POLICE ON A BURGLARY INCIDENT I, Daniel Nancy, hereby make this statement to the police concerning a burglary incident I witnessed at a department store situated along Ijebu Road, Lagos, on the night of 18th June, 2026. On the said night, I had attended a group study session with some classmates in preparation for our forthcoming examinations. I was on my way home at about 9:45 p.m. when I decided to pass through the street where the department store is located because it was the most direct route to my house. The area is usually quiet at that time of night, with only a few pedestrians and occasional vehicles passing by. As I approached the store, I noticed something unusual at the rear side of the building. At first, I thought it might be one of the security guards carrying out routine checks, but on closer observation from a concealed position behind a parked vehicle, I realised that two men were tampering with the back door of the store. One of them was forcefully trying to break the padlock using an iron rod, while the other stood a short distance away acting as a lookout, frequently turning his head to monitor the surroundings. After a few minutes of persistent effort, they succeeded in breaking the lock and gained entry into the store through the rear door. I was shocked and frightened by what I was seeing, but I ensured that I remained hidden so that I would not attract their attention or put myself in danger. Shortly after entering, I observed them switching on torchlights to navigate inside the building. They moved quickly but cautiously, picking valuable items from the shelves. I could see them packing cartons of goods, including electronics such as small home appliances, and bundles of clothing materials into large sacks which they had apparently brought along for the operation. Their movements suggested that they were well organised and familiar with the layout of the store. Realising the seriousness of the situation, I immediately left the scene and rushed to a nearby filling station where I met a security guard on duty. I informed him about the ongoing burglary and urged him to call the police immediately. He quickly contacted the nearest police station while I returned to keep a safe distance from the store to monitor developments. A few minutes later, I heard the sound of approaching sirens, which alerted the burglars. In panic, they hurriedly began to exit the store with some of the stolen goods. However, in their haste, they dropped part of the items near the back exit and fled through a narrow alley behind the building before the police could apprehend them. When the police arrived, I identified myself as the eyewitness and gave them a detailed account of everything I had observed. I also provided descriptions of the suspects: one was tall and slim, wearing a dark hooded jacket, while the other was shorter, slightly built, and wore a red cap. I also mentioned that the shorter one appeared to have a slight limp in his right leg. The police officers inspected the scene, collected the abandoned items as evidence, and assured me that investigations would continue to track down the culprits. I fully cooperated with them and offered to assist further if needed. This is my honest and voluntary statement regarding the burglary incident I witnessed. Signed, Daniel Nancy Witness

When his first offspring showed up nine months later, however, Adiga was beside himself with joy. The law enforcement officer had set himself the ambition of reaching the peak of his career using every legitimate means. And he wanted no encumbrances. With his mother's passing in 1948, Adiga became an orphan, left with no one else but his older brother, Tako. Half a decade earlier, their father had joined his ancestors after a snake bite on his depleted cocoa farm. In the last few years of her life, their mother had been bedridden with a host of ailments. Adiga had devoted himself to attending to her daily needs, including clearing her waste and bathing her. "My son," she would say, looking at him with weary eyes full of love and pity; "you shall succeed in life and no enemy will pull you down." In a tremulous voice, Adiga would answer, "Amen, thank you, Mama." On those occasions, he used to fear the worst. Looking skywards, he would ask, "God, is it time?" Because he was way older than the other pupils but quite hardworking and eager to learn, his teachers would alert him before the school inspectors arrived. Within minutes, Adiga would head for the closest bush path, returning only about an hour later.
